extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, students and researchers interested in media/journalism practices
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the media scrum as an improvised press-conference practice: what it is, where it occurs, characteristic behaviours, risks (unplanned/controversial remarks), and tactics politicians use to manage or avoid it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: improvised press conference
rubrics_metrics.description: A media scrum is an improvised press conference, often held immediately outside an event such as a legislative session or meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs informally and on-the-spot; not a scheduled or formal briefing. The informality is a defining feature and shapes expectations about spontaneity and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting: proximity to events/exit points
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrums are frequently held immediately outside events (for example, in the hallway outside the House of Commons) or as politicians exit chambers/meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The physical proximity to the event/exit concentrates reporters and enables rapid questioning as officials move between spaces; location influences accessibility and level of control possible by the public figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant behaviour: clustering and competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters cluster around a public figure competing for attention, analogous to a rugby scrum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This close clustering produces a competitive, often chaotic dynamic where multiple journalists attempt to get questions/answers simultaneously; the metaphor explains why the term 'scrum' is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic/terminology variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrums play a central role in Canadian politics and also occur in the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia and New Zealand; in New Zealand they are also called media stand-ups or gaggles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology and prominence vary by country and political culture; awareness of local names and norms is important for practitioners and observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk: disorganization leading to unplanned or controversial remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: The disorganization and pressure of the scrum makes it notorious for drawing remarks that are unplanned or controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include notable off-the-cuff comments that generated controversy. This risk is a key trade-off of scrums: access and spontaneity versus loss of message control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation strategy: avoid scrums in favour of formal venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of concerns about unplanned/controversial remarks, politicians have sometimes tried to avoid the scrum in favour of more formal venues (e.g., daily press conference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding a scheduled press conference gives more control over messaging and reduces the chance of off-the-cuff controversy; however it may reduce immediacy and accessibility to reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation tactic: positional control ("staircase scrum")
rubrics_metrics.description: Some politicians restrict or manage scrums by physical positioning (for example, standing on a stairway above reporters) to limit chaotic access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tactic can reduce reporters' ability to swarm and can change the power dynamic, but may provoke negative press reaction or accusations of avoiding accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential benefit: producing memorable soundbites
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrums can yield quick, memorable, quotable remarks (soundbites); skilled interlocutors may deflect or return barbs effectively and create lasting political quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For politicians comfortable with spontaneity, scrums offer opportunities for effective off-the-cuff communication and to shape narratives with striking lines; for novices, they pose higher risk.
